opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think checking correctness is really one of the central things, and it's maybe underappreciated in a lot of the current conversation about scaling.

The way I think about it is that there's a real asymmetry between generating something and verifying it. If you're writing a program, a world model, or a chain of reasoning, producing a candidate can be extraordinarily hard. But once you have a candidate, you can often check it relatively cheaply. You run the program on test cases. You simulate the world model and see whether it predicts what actually happens. You check whether a proof step follows. That asymmetry is what makes search work. You can afford to be a bit wild and creative in what you propose, because you have a filter on the back end that keeps you honest.

For programs specifically, this is one of the things I find most appealing about representing knowledge as code. A program is a hypothesis you can execute. If I learn a world model as a program, I can roll it forward, compare it against observations, and get a crisp signal about where it's wrong. Compare that with a big opaque neural representation, where it's much harder to say what the model believes, let alone whether that belief is right.

I'd add a couple of caveats, though. First, checking is only as good as your specification. Tests can be incomplete, and observations can be consistent with many hypotheses. So you still need some kind of prior, some notion of simplicity or naturalness, to choose among the hypotheses that pass. Verification narrows things down but doesn't uniquely pin down the answer. That's where the Bayesian or Occam's razor side comes back in.

Second, in a lot of domains we care about, there isn't a clean verifier. You can't unit test "is this a good scientific theory" or "is this a reasonable plan in an open-ended world" the way you can test a sorting function. So part of the research challenge is finding partial or approximate checks: consistency checks, predictive checks against data, self-consistency across multiple samples, or learned critics. Then you have to be careful about how much to trust them, because a learned verifier can be gamed just like anything else.

I'd also say checking isn't just a filter at the end. It can be part of the learning loop. If a system proposes hypotheses, checks them, and then learns from which ones succeeded and failed, it gets better at proposing over time. That kind of bootstrapping, where verification feeds back into a better generator and then into better abstractions, is one of the more promising paths toward systems that genuinely learn new things rather than just interpolating what they've seen.

So it's central, but it isn't the whole story. You need good generation, good priors, and good checking all working together, and much of the interesting work is in how those pieces talk to each other.

r001.rationale: The response says many important domains lack a clean verifier and identifies finding and trusting partial or approximate checks as a research challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think checking is actually central, and it's maybe the thing I've come to believe most strongly over the last few years of doing this work.

If you look at what's distinctive about programs as a representation, compared to, say, a big neural network that's implicitly modeling the world, it's not just that programs are interpretable or compositional, although those matter. It's that programs come with a notion of being wrong in a very crisp way. You can run them. You can execute a world model forward and compare what it predicts against what actually happened, and when they disagree you get a signal that's not fuzzy. It's a counterexample. And the moment you have counterexamples, you can do something really different from gradient descent, which is you can go look at the specific thing that broke and ask, what would I have to change so that this particular case works?

That's roughly how a lot of our work on learning world models in a program-like way has gone. You have a hypothesis, you have a verifier, broadly construed, and the loop is: propose, check, find the failure, revise. The checking is what lets you learn from very little data. A human playing a new video game doesn't need ten thousand episodes to figure out that touching the spiky thing is bad. They see it once, their model was wrong, they patch it. You can only do that if your model is the kind of thing that can be checked against a single observation.

The thing I'd push on, though, is that people sometimes treat checking as this clean, binary oracle, like the unit tests either pass or they don't. And for a lot of the interesting problems, that's not what you get. For world models, your observations are partial and noisy. For reasoning, the thing you're verifying is often, does this argument actually establish this conclusion, and that's not something you can always compile. So I think of correctness checking as a spectrum. On one end you have formal verification, proofs, executing code against tests. On the other end you have something more like a learned critic, or just the model noticing an inconsistency with something else it believes. Both of those are checking. The formal end is more trustworthy but applies to fewer problems, and the soft end applies everywhere but can be fooled.

And where I think the field is heading, and where I've been trying to push, is building systems that can sit in the middle. Use a language model to propose, because that's what they're good at, generating plausible structured hypotheses from priors over how the world tends to work. But then don't just trust the proposal. Try to ground it in something executable, something you can actually test. If the model proposes that an object in a game behaves a certain way, write that down as code and simulate it. If it proposes a reasoning step, see if you can turn it into something a solver can confirm. The hard part, and honestly the research question, is how much of the problem you can get into that checkable form, because the more you can, the less you're relying on the model just being right.

The other role of checking, which I think is underrated, is that it's what makes learning cumulative. If you have verified pieces, you can build on them. Library learning, this idea of a system that accumulates reusable abstractions over time, only really works if the things in the library are actually correct, because otherwise your errors compound. So checking isn't just about getting the current answer right. It's about having a foundation you can trust enough to keep building on top of.

r001.rationale: The response says correctness checks are unavailable or imperfect for some problems, describes learned critics and inconsistency checks as softer alternatives, and identifies how much of a problem can be made checkable as an open research question.

astra-6.text:
I think a really useful distinction is between generating a candidate explanation and checking that explanation. It can be very difficult to come up with a program that solves a problem, but once you have a candidate, you can run it and see what it does. That gives learning a powerful source of feedback beyond whether the candidate looks like something a person would write.

With world models, the situation is a little less clean. You can check whether a model predicts an observation, but getting that prediction right doesn’t establish that the model is correct in general. There might be several explanations consistent with everything you’ve seen. So you need to ask what experiment or intervention would distinguish them. Checking becomes part of an ongoing process of discovering where your model fails.

For reasoning systems, I’d like to exploit that same loop: propose something, derive consequences, check those consequences, and revise. A proof checker gives you a particularly strong version of this, because it can establish that a conclusion follows from specified assumptions. Running a program on a few examples gives you a weaker version, but it’s still useful.

The important question is what your check actually warrants. Passing tests isn’t the same as proving correctness, and proving something about a model isn’t the same as showing that the model describes the world. But even imperfect checks can make learning much more effective, provided the system can use failures to improve its next proposal.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes checks, experiments, and feedback as useful ways to improve proposals, but it does not identify training systems when correctness cannot be checked as an unresolved research problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think checking is a really important part of the story, because producing a candidate solution and knowing whether it works are often very different problems. If I write a program, I can run it. That gives me a way to learn from something other than whether the program looks like programs I’ve seen before.

But there are different strengths of checking. Passing a few tests doesn’t establish that a program is correct. And with a world model, agreement with the observations you already have doesn’t mean you’ve learned the right underlying mechanism. You want to ask: what new prediction does this model make, and what experiment would distinguish it from another model that also explains the data?

So I’d like learning and checking to be in a loop. You propose an explanation or a program, derive some consequences, check those consequences, and use the failures to guide what you propose next. Reasoning is useful there because it lets you work out consequences that aren’t immediately apparent from the representation.

The caveat is that the checker has to get its authority from somewhere. If it’s just another learned model saying, ‘Yes, that sounds plausible,’ you can have correlated mistakes. Execution, interaction with the world, and formal proof offer different kinds of grounding. The interesting question is how to combine those with learning so that we can discover things we don’t already know how to verify completely.

r001.rationale: The response says the checker’s authority must come from somewhere and frames combining grounded checks with learning to discover things that cannot yet be verified completely as an open question.
